# Answer in brief

* **The first claim (systems of equations) is TRUE, but the proof given for it is not.** Adding two
  equations yields a *consequence* of the system, never an equivalent of it, so the inductive step
  as written is false (Example 2.4). A correct merging step is supplied by the Bézout identity /
  greatest common right divisor in the ring $K[\partial]$ of linear differential operators; with it,
  the induction on $n$ goes through exactly in the shape intended (Lemma 2.1, Theorem A).

* **The second claim (systems of inequations) is FALSE.** The questioner's own worry ("what if
  $a=-b$?") is fatal, and the proposed remedy ("assume $a,b>0$") cannot work. Already
  $x\ne 0\wedge x\ne 1$ is not equivalent to $Lx\ne g$ conjoined with any $x$-free condition
  (Theorem B). Theorem C determines exactly when such a merging is possible: only in the degenerate
  case where one of the inequations already implies all the others.

* Section 5 states the repaired formulation and the substitute result that is actually usable
  (Corollary 5.1: inequations can be reduced *modulo* the equation).

---

# 0. Setting, conventions, and the precise statements

Throughout, $(K,\partial)$ is a differential field of characteristic $0$; thus $\mathbb{Q}\subseteq K$
and $\partial$ vanishes on $\mathbb{Q}$. Let $F$ be a commutative differential ring extension of $K$:
$K\subseteq F$, and the derivation of $F$ (also written $\partial$, or $y\mapsto y'$) restricts on
$K$ to $\partial$. The unknown $x$ ranges over $F$, and the right-hand sides $f_j,g_j$ are elements of
$F$. Typical instances: $K=\mathbb{Q}(t)$ with $\partial=d/dt$ and $F=K$, or $F$ any differential
field extension of $K$; or $K=\mathbb{R}$ with the zero derivation and $F=C^{\infty}(\mathbb{R})$
with $\partial=d/dt$ (constant–coefficient operators acting on smooth functions).

By a *differential operator* we mean a **linear** one, i.e. an element of the ring
$K[\partial]$ of linear differential operators, defined as follows. As a left $K$-module,
$$K[\partial]=\bigoplus_{i\ge0}K\partial^{i}
=\Big\{\textstyle\sum_{i=0}^{m}a_i\partial^{i}\;:\;m\in\mathbb{N},\ a_i\in K\Big\}$$
is free with basis $(\partial^i)_{i\ge0}$ (so two such expressions are equal iff their coefficients
agree), and multiplication is the unique $\mathbb{Z}$-bilinear, associative, unital multiplication
with $\partial^i\cdot\partial^j=\partial^{i+j}$ extending that of $K$ and satisfying the commutation
rule
$$\partial\cdot a=a\,\partial+a'\qquad(a\in K).$$
(This is the Ore extension $K[\partial;\mathrm{id},\partial]$; its existence and associativity are
standard and are not re-proved here.) We write $\deg A$ for the order of $A=\sum_ia_i\partial^i$,
i.e. the largest $i$ with $a_i\ne0$, with $\deg 0=-\infty$, and we call $a_{\deg A}$ the leading coefficient
of $A\ne0$. Linearity of the $L_j$ is exactly what the phrase "we add these two equations"
presupposes, so this is the intended reading; see also Remark 3.3.

Operators are *applied* to elements of $F$ by
$$Ay:=\sum_{i}a_iy^{(i)}\qquad\Big(A=\sum_ia_i\partial^i\in K[\partial],\ y\in F\Big),$$
where $y^{(i)}$ denotes the $i$-th derivative of $y$ in $F$. Lemma 1.0 below checks that this is an
action, i.e. that $(AB)y=A(By)$; we do *not* need the action to be faithful (it need not be, e.g.
when the derivation of $F$ is trivial).

**Reading of the claims.** "$\phi$ can be written as $Lx=f\wedge\psi$, where $\psi$ does not contain
any $x$" means: there exist $L\in K[\partial]$, $f\in F$ and a condition $\psi$ in which $x$ does not
occur, such that
$$\text{for all }x\in F:\qquad \phi(x)\iff\big(Lx=f\ \wedge\ \psi\big). \tag{0.1}$$
The data $L_1,\dots,L_n$ and $f_1,\dots,f_n$ (resp. $g_1,\dots,g_n$) are fixed, and $x$ does not
occur in $\psi$; hence $\psi$ has a definite truth value, and the solution set of the right-hand side
of (0.1) is
$$\{x\in F:\ Lx=f\ \wedge\ \psi\}=\begin{cases}\{x\in F: Lx=f\}, & \psi\ \text{true},\\[2pt]
\emptyset, & \psi\ \text{false.}\end{cases}\tag{0.2}$$
This is the only consequence of "$\psi$ does not contain $x$" that will be used. (If the $f_j,g_j$
are themselves terms in further variables $\bar y$, then (0.1) is to be read for each fixed value of
$\bar y$; all positive results below are uniform in $\bar y$, and the counterexamples below use data
in which no $\bar y$ occurs, so nothing is lost. We analyse the two displayed assertions as they
stand, i.e. as equivalences of formulas; no claim is made here about variants in which $\phi$ is
placed under an existential quantifier.)

The two assertions under discussion are therefore:

> **Claim 1.** For all $n\ge1$, $L_1,\dots,L_n\in K[\partial]$ and $f_1,\dots,f_n\in F$ there exist
> $L\in K[\partial]$, $f\in F$ and an $x$-free condition $\psi$ such that for all $x\in F$
> $$\bigwedge_{j=1}^{n}L_jx=f_j\iff\big(Lx=f\wedge\psi\big).$$
>
> **Claim 2.** For all $n\ge1$, $L_1,\dots,L_n\in K[\partial]$ and $g_1,\dots,g_n\in F$ there exist
> $L\in K[\partial]$, $g\in F$ and an $x$-free condition $\psi$ such that for all $x\in F$
> $$\bigwedge_{j=1}^{n}L_jx\neq g_j\iff\big(Lx\neq g\wedge\psi\big).$$

Claim 1 is true (Theorem A). Claim 2 is false (Theorem B), and Theorem C says exactly when a system
of inequations admits such a reduction.

We shall use constantly the two evaluation rules: for $A,B\in K[\partial]$ and $y,z\in F$,
$$y=z\ \Longrightarrow\ Ay=Az\qquad\text{(because $A$ is a map $F\to F$)},\qquad (AB)y=A(By)
\qquad\text{(Lemma 1.0)} .$$

---

# 1. Preliminaries on the ring $K[\partial]$

**Lemma 1.0 (operators act).** *For all $A,B\in K[\partial]$ and $y,z\in F$:*
$$A(y+z)=Ay+Az,\qquad (A+B)y=Ay+By,\qquad (AB)y=A(By).$$
*Thus $A\mapsto(y\mapsto Ay)$ is a homomorphism from $K[\partial]$ to the ring of additive
endomorphisms of $F$.*

*Proof.* The first two identities are immediate from the definition $Ay=\sum_ia_iy^{(i)}$, since
$y\mapsto y^{(i)}$ is additive and multiplication in $F$ is distributive.

For the third, both $(A,B)\mapsto(AB)y$ and $(A,B)\mapsto A(By)$ are additive in $A$ and in $B$
(for the latter, use that $B\mapsto By$ is additive and that $A$ acts additively on $F$, which is the
first identity). Since $K[\partial]$ is generated additively by the elements $a\partial^k$
$(a\in K,k\ge0)$, it suffices to treat $A=a\partial^{k}$, $B=b\partial^{l}$. By Lemma 1.1 below
(whose proof uses only the commutation rule, not Lemma 1.0),
$$AB=a\partial^{k}b\,\partial^{l}=\sum_{i=0}^{k}\binom{k}{i}ab^{(i)}\partial^{\,k-i+l},$$
so $(AB)y=\sum_{i=0}^{k}\binom{k}{i}ab^{(i)}y^{(k-i+l)}$. On the other hand, by the Leibniz rule in
the differential ring $F$,
$$A(By)=a\big(b\,y^{(l)}\big)^{(k)}=a\sum_{i=0}^{k}\binom{k}{i}b^{(i)}\big(y^{(l)}\big)^{(k-i)}
=\sum_{i=0}^{k}\binom{k}{i}ab^{(i)}y^{(k-i+l)} .$$
The two agree. $\square$

**Lemma 1.1.** *For $a\in K$ and $k\in\mathbb{N}$ one has
$\partial^{k}\cdot a=\sum_{i=0}^{k}\binom{k}{i}a^{(i)}\partial^{\,k-i}$ in $K[\partial]$; in
particular $\partial^k\cdot a$ has degree $k$ and leading coefficient $a$ when $a \neq 0$. Consequently, for all
$A,B\in K[\partial]$ one has $\deg(AB)=\deg A+\deg B$, the leading coefficient of $AB$ is the
product of the leading coefficients of $A$ and $B$ when $A,B\ne0$, and $K[\partial]$ is an integral
domain (non-commutative in general).*

*Proof.* The formula for $\partial^k\cdot a$ follows by induction on $k$ from
$\partial\cdot a=a\partial+a'$: it holds for $k=0$, and
$$\partial^{k+1}\!\cdot a=\partial\cdot\Big(\sum_{i}\binom{k}{i}a^{(i)}\partial^{k-i}\Big)
=\sum_{i}\binom{k}{i}\big(a^{(i)}\partial^{k+1-i}+a^{(i+1)}\partial^{k-i}\big)
=\sum_{i}\binom{k+1}{i}a^{(i)}\partial^{k+1-i},$$
by Pascal's rule.

For the degree formula we may assume $A,B\neq0$ (otherwise both sides are $-\infty$). Write
$A=\sum_{i\le m}a_i\partial^i$ with $a_m\ne0$ and $B=\sum_{j\le d}b_j\partial^j$ with $b_d\ne0$. Then
$AB=\sum_{i\le m,\ j\le d}a_i\partial^{i}b_j\partial^{j}$, and by the first part
$a_i\partial^ib_j\partial^j=a_ib_j\partial^{i+j}+(\text{terms of degree}<i+j)$. Since $i\le m$ and
$j\le d$, we have $i+j\le m+d$ with equality only for $(i,j)=(m,d)$. Hence the coefficient of
$\partial^{m+d}$ in $AB$ is $a_mb_d$, which is nonzero because $K$ is a field, and all other terms
have degree $<m+d$. So $\deg(AB)=m+d$, the leading coefficient of $AB$ is $a_mb_d$, and $AB\ne0$. $\square$

**Lemma 1.2 (right division with remainder).** *Let $A,B\in K[\partial]$ with $B\neq0$. Then there
are $Q,R\in K[\partial]$ with*
$$A=QB+R,\qquad \deg R<\deg B .$$

*Proof.* Strong induction on $\deg A$. If $\deg A<\deg B$, take $Q=0$, $R=A$. Otherwise write
$A=a_m\partial^m+(\text{lower})$ with $a_m\neq0$, $B=b_d\partial^d+(\text{lower})$ with $b_d\neq0$
and $m\ge d$. By Lemma 1.1, $\partial^{m-d}B$ has degree $m$ and leading coefficient $b_d$, so
$\frac{a_m}{b_d}\partial^{m-d}B$ has degree $m$ and leading coefficient $a_m$; hence
$\tilde A:=A-\frac{a_m}{b_d}\partial^{m-d}B$ has $\deg\tilde A<m$. By the inductive hypothesis
$\tilde A=\tilde QB+R$ with $\deg R<\deg B$, and then
$A=\big(\tfrac{a_m}{b_d}\partial^{m-d}+\tilde Q\big)B+R$. $\square$

**Lemma 1.3 (left ideals are principal; Bézout).** *Let $n\ge1$ and $A_1,\dots,A_n\in K[\partial]$,
and let $I:=K[\partial]A_1+\dots+K[\partial]A_n$ be the left ideal they generate. Then $I=K[\partial]L$
for some $L\in K[\partial]$, and there exist $U_1,\dots,U_n,V_1,\dots,V_n\in K[\partial]$ with*
$$L=\sum_{j=1}^{n}U_jA_j\qquad\text{and}\qquad A_j=V_jL\ \ (1\le j\le n).$$

*Proof.* Note first that $I=\big\{\sum_{j}U_jA_j\ :\ U_j\in K[\partial]\big\}$, since the right-hand
side is a left ideal (it is closed under addition and under left multiplication) which contains each
$A_j$ (take $U_j=1$ and the others $0$) and is contained in $I$.

If $I=\{0\}$, then every $A_j=0$; take $L=0$ and $U_j=V_j=0$. Otherwise choose $L\in I\setminus\{0\}$
of minimal degree. Then $K[\partial]L\subseteq I$. Conversely, let $A\in I$ and write $A=QL+R$ with
$\deg R<\deg L$ (Lemma 1.2). Then $R=A-QL\in I$, so minimality of $\deg L$ forces $R=0$, i.e.
$A\in K[\partial]L$. Hence $I=K[\partial]L$. The $U_j$ exist because $L\in I$, and the $V_j$ exist
because $A_j\in I=K[\partial]L$. $\square$

Such an $L$ is a *greatest common right divisor* $\mathrm{GCRD}(A_1,\dots,A_n)$; it is unique up to
left multiplication by an element of $K^\times$, and Lemma 1.2 provides a Euclidean algorithm to
compute it together with the $U_j$ and $V_j$.

---

# 2. Claim 1 is true — but not for the reason given

## 2.1 A correct proof, in the intended inductive shape

**Lemma 2.1 (merging two equations).** *Let $A_1,A_2\in K[\partial]$ and $h_1,h_2\in F$. Then there
exist $L\in K[\partial]$, $f\in F$ and $V_1,V_2\in K[\partial]$ such that for all $x\in F$*
$$\big(A_1x=h_1\ \wedge\ A_2x=h_2\big)\iff\big(Lx=f\ \wedge\ V_1f=h_1\ \wedge\ V_2f=h_2\big),$$
*and the last two conjuncts do not involve $x$.*

*Proof.* By Lemma 1.3 (with $n=2$) choose $L$ with $K[\partial]A_1+K[\partial]A_2=K[\partial]L$, and
$U_1,U_2,V_1,V_2$ with
$$L=U_1A_1+U_2A_2,\qquad A_1=V_1L,\qquad A_2=V_2L .$$
Put $f:=U_1h_1+U_2h_2\in F$.

($\Rightarrow$) Assume $A_1x=h_1$ and $A_2x=h_2$. Applying $U_i$ to the $i$-th equation and adding,
$$Lx=(U_1A_1+U_2A_2)x=U_1(A_1x)+U_2(A_2x)=U_1h_1+U_2h_2=f .$$
Moreover, for $i=1,2$: $V_if=V_i(Lx)=(V_iL)x=A_ix=h_i$.

($\Leftarrow$) Assume $Lx=f$ and $V_1f=h_1$, $V_2f=h_2$. Then for $i=1,2$,
$$A_ix=(V_iL)x=V_i(Lx)=V_if=h_i.\qquad\square$$

No case distinction is needed: the proof covers also $A_1=A_2=0$ (then $L=0$, $f=0$, $V_i=0$, and
both sides of the equivalence say $h_1=h_2=0$).

**Theorem A.** *Claim 1 holds: for every $n\ge1$, all $L_1,\dots,L_n\in K[\partial]$ and
$f_1,\dots,f_n\in F$, there are $L\in K[\partial]$, $f\in F$ and a condition $\psi$ not containing
$x$ — in fact a finite conjunction of equalities between elements of $F$ — such that*
$$\text{for all }x\in F:\qquad\bigwedge_{j=1}^{n}L_jx=f_j\iff\big(Lx=f\ \wedge\ \psi\big).$$

*Proof, by induction on $n$ (the structure intended in the question).*

*Base case $n=1$.* Take $L=L_1$, $f=f_1$ and $\psi$ the true $x$-free condition $f_1=f_1$.

*Induction step.* Assume the statement for some $k\ge1$, and let $L_1,\dots,L_{k+1}\in K[\partial]$,
$f_1,\dots,f_{k+1}\in F$ be given. By the inductive hypothesis applied to the first $k$ equations
there are $\hat L\in K[\partial]$, $\hat f\in F$ and an $x$-free $\hat\psi$ with
$$\bigwedge_{j=1}^{k}L_jx=f_j\iff\big(\hat Lx=\hat f\ \wedge\ \hat\psi\big)\qquad(\forall x\in F).$$
Conjoining $L_{k+1}x=f_{k+1}$ to both sides,
$$\bigwedge_{j=1}^{k+1}L_jx=f_j\iff\big(\hat Lx=\hat f\ \wedge\ L_{k+1}x=f_{k+1}\ \wedge\ \hat\psi\big)
\qquad(\forall x\in F).$$
Apply Lemma 2.1 to $A_1=\hat L,h_1=\hat f$ and $A_2=L_{k+1},h_2=f_{k+1}$: there are $L,f$ and $V,W$
with
$$\big(\hat Lx=\hat f\wedge L_{k+1}x=f_{k+1}\big)\iff\big(Lx=f\ \wedge\ Vf=\hat f\ \wedge\ Wf=f_{k+1}\big)
\qquad(\forall x\in F).$$
Substituting, we get for all $x\in F$
$$\bigwedge_{j=1}^{k+1}L_jx=f_j\iff\big(Lx=f\ \wedge\ \psi\big),\qquad
\psi:\equiv\big(Vf=\hat f\ \wedge\ Wf=f_{k+1}\ \wedge\ \hat\psi\big),$$
and $x$ occurs in none of the conjuncts of $\psi$ (in $\hat\psi$ by the inductive hypothesis, in the
other two by construction). This completes the induction. $\square$

## 2.2 The closed form: what $L$, $f$ and $\psi$ really are

**Theorem A$'$ (non-inductive version, with explicit data).** *Let $n\ge1$,
$L_1,\dots,L_n\in K[\partial]$, $f_1,\dots,f_n\in F$. Choose, by Lemma 1.3,
$L=\mathrm{GCRD}(L_1,\dots,L_n)$ generating $\sum_{j}K[\partial]L_j$, together with $U_j,V_j$ such
that $L=\sum_jU_jL_j$ and $L_j=V_jL$, and put $f:=\sum_{j}U_jf_j$. Then for all $x\in F$*
$$\bigwedge_{j=1}^{n}L_jx=f_j\iff\Big(Lx=f\ \wedge\ \bigwedge_{j=1}^{n}V_jf=f_j\Big).$$

*Proof.* ($\Rightarrow$) If $L_jx=f_j$ for all $j$, then
$Lx=\big(\sum_jU_jL_j\big)x=\sum_jU_j(L_jx)=\sum_jU_jf_j=f$, and consequently
$V_jf=V_j(Lx)=(V_jL)x=L_jx=f_j$ for each $j$.

($\Leftarrow$) If $Lx=f$ and $V_jf=f_j$ for all $j$, then $L_jx=(V_jL)x=V_j(Lx)=V_jf=f_j$. $\square$

So the correct "$L$" is a greatest common right divisor of $L_1,\dots,L_n$ (computable by the
non-commutative Euclidean algorithm of Lemma 1.2), $f$ is the corresponding Bézout combination of
the right-hand sides, and $\psi$ is the compatibility condition $\bigwedge_jV_jf=f_j$.

**Example 2.2.** For the system $x'=f_1\wedge x=f_2$ we have $L_1=\partial$, $L_2=1$, and
$\mathrm{GCRD}(\partial,1)=1$ with $1=0\cdot\partial+1\cdot 1$, $\partial=\partial\cdot 1$,
$1=1\cdot1$; thus $L=1$, $f=f_2$, $V_1=\partial$, $V_2=1$, and Theorem A$'$ gives
$$x'=f_1\wedge x=f_2\iff\big(x=f_2\ \wedge\ f_2'=f_1\big),$$
which is visibly correct. Note that the *sum* of the two equations, $x'+x=f_1+f_2$, is merely a
consequence of the system and in general not equivalent to it (Example 2.4).

## 2.3 Why the proof given in the question fails

Two separate things go wrong in the inductive step "we add these two equations and we get a new
differential equation $Lx=f$; so the initial system is equivalent to the new differential equation".

1. **Adding is not an equivalence.** For $A_1,A_2\in K[\partial]$, $h_1,h_2\in F$ one has only the
   inclusion
   $$\{x: A_1x=h_1\}\cap\{x: A_2x=h_2\}\ \subseteq\ \{x:(A_1+A_2)x=h_1+h_2\},$$
   and this inclusion is in general strict (Example 2.4). The reverse implication — the one needed
   for an equivalence — is simply not available: one equation cannot in general be split back into
   two.

2. **The side condition is discarded.** Even with a correct merging step one must carry the
   previously produced $\psi$, and the newly produced side conditions, along; compare the induction
   step of Theorem A. The conclusion "the initial system is equivalent to $Lx=f$" (with no $\psi$)
   is not the statement to be proved, and is false in general.

**Example 2.4 (the summing step is genuinely wrong).** Let $K=F=\mathbb{Q}(t)$, $\partial=d/dt$, and
$$\phi:\quad x'=1\ \wedge\ x=0 .$$
$\phi$ has no solution in $F$ at all: $x=0$ gives $x'=0\ne1$. Its sum is $x'+x=1$, which *is*
satisfied, e.g. by $x=1$. Hence $\phi$ is not equivalent to the summed equation, and the inductive
step as written would "prove" an unsatisfiable system equivalent to a satisfiable one. (A second
illustration: over $K=\mathbb{R}$, $F=C^\infty(\mathbb{R})$, the system $x=0\wedge x'=0$ forces
$x=0$, while the summed equation $x+x'=0$ is solved by every $x=c\,e^{-t}$, $c\in\mathbb{R}$.)

This refutes the *proof*, not the *statement*: by Theorem A$'$ the system of Example 2.4 is
equivalent to $x=0\wedge 0=1$ — indeed $L=\mathrm{GCRD}(\partial,1)=1$, $f=0\cdot 1+1\cdot 0=0$,
$V_1=\partial$, $V_2=1$, so $\psi$ is $(\partial 0=1)\wedge(0=0)$, i.e. the false $x$-free condition
$0=1$, which correctly records the unsatisfiability of $\phi$.

---

# 3. Claim 2 is false

The structural point is that the solution set of a single equation is an affine subspace over the
constants — hence "$0$, $1$ or infinitely many points" — whereas the negation of a system of $n$
inequations describes a union of $n$ such sets.

**Lemma 3.1.** *Let $L\in K[\partial]$ and $g\in F$. Then $L:F\to F$ is $\mathbb{Q}$-linear, and*
$$Z(L,g):=\{x\in F:\ Lx=g\}$$
*is either empty or a coset $x_0+\ker_FL$ of the $\mathbb{Q}$-subspace $\ker_FL:=\{y\in F: Ly=0\}$
of $F$. In particular $Z(L,g)$ is empty, or a singleton, or infinite.*

*Proof.* $F$ is a commutative ring containing the field $\mathbb{Q}$ (as $\mathbb{Q}\subseteq K
\subseteq F$ and $1\neq0$ in $F$), hence a $\mathbb{Q}$-vector space. The derivation $\partial$ is
additive and kills $\mathbb{Q}$, so $\partial(qy)=q\,\partial y$ for $q\in\mathbb{Q},y\in F$;
multiplication by $a\in K$ is additive and commutes with multiplication by $q$. Hence every
$L\in K[\partial]$ is additive with $L(qy)=qLy$, i.e. $\mathbb{Q}$-linear.

If $x_0\in Z(L,g)$ then for any $x$: $Lx=g\iff L(x-x_0)=0$, so $Z(L,g)=x_0+\ker_FL$. Finally
$\ker_FL$ is a $\mathbb{Q}$-subspace; if it contains some $y\ne0$, the elements $qy$ $(q\in\mathbb{Q})$
are pairwise distinct, so $\ker_FL$ is infinite; otherwise $\ker_FL=\{0\}$ and $Z(L,g)$ is empty or a
singleton. $\square$

**Theorem B.** *Claim 2 is false. Explicitly, take $n=2$, $L_1=L_2=1$ (the identity operator),
$g_1=0$, $g_2=1$, i.e.*
$$\phi:\quad x\neq0\ \wedge\ x\neq1 ,$$
*for any $K$ and $F$ as in \S0 (e.g. $K=F=\mathbb{Q}(t)$, or $K=\mathbb{R}$ and
$F=C^\infty(\mathbb{R})$).
Then there are no $L\in K[\partial]$, $g\in F$ and $x$-free condition $\psi$ such that
$\phi(x)\iff(Lx\ne g\wedge\psi)$ for all $x\in F$.*

*Proof.* Suppose such $L,g,\psi$ existed. By (0.2) there are two cases.

*Case 1: $\psi$ is false.* Then $Lx\ne g\wedge\psi$ holds for no $x$, while $x=2$ satisfies $\phi$:
indeed $2\ne0$ and $2\ne1$ in $F$, since $\mathbb{Q}\subseteq F$ and $F$ has characteristic $0$.
Contradiction.

*Case 2: $\psi$ is true.* Then $\{x\in F:\ x\ne0\wedge x\ne1\}=\{x\in F:\ Lx\ne g\}$; taking
complements in $F$,
$$\{0,1\}=Z(L,g).$$
This set is nonempty, so by Lemma 3.1 it is a coset of $\ker_FL$; as $0\in Z(L,g)$ we may take
$x_0=0$, giving $\ker_FL=Z(L,g)=\{0,1\}$. But $\ker_FL$ is a $\mathbb{Q}$-subspace containing $1$,
hence contains $2=2\cdot1$, and $2\notin\{0,1\}$ because $\operatorname{char}F=0$. Contradiction.

As both cases are impossible, no such reduction exists. $\square$

**Remark 3.2 (diagnosis; the $a,b$ question).** The step

> "$Lx\ne g\wedge L_{k+1}x\ne g_{k+1}$ is equivalent to $L_{k+1}x=f_{k+1}+a$, $Lx=f+b$ with
> $a,b\ne0$; adding, $\tilde Lx=f_{k+1}+f+a+b$, hence $\tilde Lx\ne f_{k+1}+f$"

(we keep the question's notation, in which the right-hand sides of the two inequations are written
$f_{k+1}$ and $f$) is invalid, and the questioner's objection is exactly the right one: nothing
forbids $a+b=0$, and then $\tilde Lx=f_{k+1}+f$, so the conclusion fails. Three further comments.

* **One may not "suppose $a,b>0$".** (i) $a$ and $b$ are not free parameters: they are *determined*
  by $x$, namely $a=L_{k+1}x-f_{k+1}$ and $b=Lx-f$, and they vary with $x$ over all nonzero values
  that occur. (ii) Adding the hypothesis $a,b>0$ would replace $\phi$ by a strictly stronger formula,
  so what one proves is no longer an equivalence with $\phi$. (iii) A general differential field
  carries no ordering (e.g. $\mathbb{C}(t)$, or $\mathbb{Q}(t)$ with no order fixed), so "$a>0$" need
  not even be expressible; and where it is, e.g. $F=C^\infty(\mathbb{R})$, "$a\ne0$" is far weaker
  than "$a>0$" for functions. (iv) Decisively: by Theorem B no repair whatever can work, since the
  statement to be proved is false.
* **The implication that does hold points the wrong way.** From $Ax=h\wedge Bx=k$ one gets
  $(A+B)x=h+k$; contrapositively, $(A+B)x\ne h+k$ implies $Ax\ne h\ \vee\ Bx\ne k$. Summing therefore
  converts a *conjunction* of inequations into a *disjunction*, which is precisely the wrong shape.
  Structurally: $\{x:Lx\ne g\}$ is the complement of one affine set, while $\bigwedge_jL_jx\ne g_j$
  defines the complement of a union of $n$ affine sets.
* In the counterexample of Theorem B all operators are the identity, so no subtlety about
  differentiation is involved: the obstruction is purely affine-geometric.

**Remark 3.3 (why linearity must be assumed).** The analysis above — and the manipulation "add the
two equations" — presupposes that the $L_j$ are linear operators. If "differential operator" were
allowed to mean an arbitrary (nonlinear) map $F\to F$, the normal-form question would degenerate:
for instance over $F=C^\infty(\mathbb{R})$ the system $x\ne0\wedge x\ne1$ is $N(x)\ne0$ for the
nonlinear operator $N(x)=x(x-1)$, so Claim 2 would become true for trivial reasons and would say
nothing about differential equations. The claims are interesting, and are analysed here, for
$L_j\in K[\partial]$.

# 4. Exactly when a system of inequations can be merged

Theorem B can be sharpened into a complete criterion: a conjunction of inequations reduces to a
single inequation only in the trivial situation in which one conjunct already implies the others.

**Lemma 4.1 (a vector space is not a finite union of proper affine subspaces).** *Let $V$ be a vector
space over an infinite field $C$, and let $W_1,\dots,W_n$ $(n\ge1)$ be affine subspaces of $V$ (i.e.
cosets $w+U$ of linear subspaces $U\subseteq V$) with $V=\bigcup_{i=1}^{n}W_i$. Then $W_i=V$ for some
$i$.*

*Proof.* Suppose the lemma fails. Among all counterexamples (over all fields, spaces and families),
choose one for which $n$ is minimal; so $V=\bigcup_{i\le n}W_i$ with every $W_i\subsetneq V$, and no
vector space over an infinite field is the union of fewer than $n$ proper affine subspaces.

If $n=1$ then $V=W_1\subsetneq V$, absurd; so $n\ge2$. By minimality, $\bigcup_{i\ge2}W_i\ne V$;
choose $p\in V\setminus\bigcup_{i\ge2}W_i$. Since the $W_i$ cover $V$, necessarily $p\in W_1$. Since
$W_1\subsetneq V$, choose $q\in V\setminus W_1$; in particular $p\ne q$. Put
$$\ell:=\{q+t(p-q)\ :\ t\in C\}\subseteq V .$$
As $p-q\ne0$, the map $t\mapsto q+t(p-q)$ is injective, so $\ell$ is infinite. Note $q\in\ell$
$(t=0)$ and $p\in\ell$ $(t=1)$.

*Claim: any affine subspace $W=w+U$ containing two distinct points $a,b\in\ell$ contains all of
$\ell$.* Write $a=q+t_1(p-q)$, $b=q+t_2(p-q)$ with $t_1\ne t_2$. Then $b-a=(t_2-t_1)(p-q)\in U$
(as $a,b\in w+U$), hence $p-q=(t_2-t_1)^{-1}(b-a)\in U$ and therefore
$\ell=a+\{(t-t_1)(p-q):t\in C\}\subseteq a+U=w+U=W$.

Now $q\in\ell\setminus W_1$, so $\ell\not\subseteq W_1$, whence $|\ell\cap W_1|\le1$ by the Claim.
For $i\ge2$ we have $p\in\ell\setminus W_i$, so likewise $|\ell\cap W_i|\le1$. Therefore
$\ell=\ell\cap V=\bigcup_{i=1}^{n}(\ell\cap W_i)$ has at most $n$ elements, contradicting that $\ell$
is infinite. $\square$

**Theorem C.** *Let $n\ge1$, $L_1,\dots,L_n\in K[\partial]$, $g_1,\dots,g_n\in F$, and set
$Z_j:=Z(L_j,g_j)=\{x\in F: L_jx=g_j\}$. The following are equivalent.*

*(1) There exist $L\in K[\partial]$, $g\in F$ and an $x$-free condition $\psi$ such that*
$$\text{for all }x\in F:\qquad\bigwedge_{j=1}^{n}L_jx\ne g_j\iff\big(Lx\ne g\ \wedge\ \psi\big).$$

*(2) There is an index $j_0$ with $Z_j\subseteq Z_{j_0}$ for all $j$; equivalently, one conjunct
already implies all the others:*
$$\text{for all }x\in F:\qquad\bigwedge_{j=1}^{n}L_jx\ne g_j\iff L_{j_0}x\ne g_{j_0}.$$

*Proof.* Throughout, view $F$ as a vector space over the infinite field $\mathbb{Q}$; by Lemma 3.1
each $Z_j$ is either empty or an affine $\mathbb{Q}$-subspace of $F$. Observe that
$\bigwedge_jL_jx\ne g_j$ holds iff $x\in F\setminus\bigcup_jZ_j$.

*The two formulations in (2) agree.* If $Z_j\subseteq Z_{j_0}$ for all $j$, then
$\bigcup_jZ_j=Z_{j_0}$, so $\bigwedge_jL_jx\ne g_j\iff x\notin Z_{j_0}\iff L_{j_0}x\ne g_{j_0}$.
Conversely, if that formula equivalence holds for all $x$, then the complements agree,
$\bigcup_jZ_j=Z_{j_0}$, whence $Z_j\subseteq Z_{j_0}$ for every $j$.

*(2)$\Rightarrow$(1).* Take $L:=L_{j_0}$, $g:=g_{j_0}$ and $\psi$ any true $x$-free condition, say
$0=0$; the required equivalence is the one just displayed.

*(1)$\Rightarrow$(2).* Assume (1) and apply (0.2).

*Case $\psi$ false.* Then $F\setminus\bigcup_jZ_j=\emptyset$, i.e. $\bigcup_jZ_j=F$. Discard the
empty $Z_j$'s; not all are empty, since $F\ne\emptyset$. The remaining ones are affine
$\mathbb{Q}$-subspaces of $F$ whose union is $F$, so Lemma 4.1 (with $V=F$, $C=\mathbb{Q}$) yields
$j_0$ with $Z_{j_0}=F$, and then $Z_j\subseteq Z_{j_0}$ for all $j$.

*Case $\psi$ true.* Then $F\setminus\bigcup_jZ_j=F\setminus Z(L,g)$, hence
$$\bigcup_{j=1}^{n}Z_j=Z(L,g)=:Z .$$
If $Z=\emptyset$, then all $Z_j$ are empty and (2) holds with $j_0=1$. Otherwise, by Lemma 3.1,
$Z=x_0+V$ with $V:=\ker_FL$ a $\mathbb{Q}$-subspace of $F$ and $x_0\in Z$. Let $J:=\{j: Z_j\ne
\emptyset\}$; $J\ne\emptyset$ because $\bigcup_jZ_j=Z\ne\emptyset$. For $j\in J$ write
$Z_j=z_j+\ker_FL_j$ (Lemma 3.1). Since $Z_j\subseteq Z=z_j+V$ (using $z_j\in Z_j\subseteq Z$), every
$y\in\ker_FL_j$ satisfies $z_j+y\in Z=z_j+V$, i.e. $\ker_FL_j\subseteq V$. Hence
$$W_j:=Z_j-x_0=(z_j-x_0)+\ker_FL_j\qquad(j\in J)$$
is an affine subspace of the $\mathbb{Q}$-vector space $V$ (note $z_j-x_0\in Z-x_0=V$), and
$\bigcup_{j\in J}W_j=\big(\bigcup_jZ_j\big)-x_0=Z-x_0=V$. By Lemma 4.1 applied to $V$ over
$\mathbb{Q}$, there is $j_0\in J$ with $W_{j_0}=V$, i.e. $Z_{j_0}=Z=\bigcup_jZ_j$, so
$Z_j\subseteq Z_{j_0}$ for all $j$. $\square$

**Corollary 4.2 (Theorem B again).** For $\phi:\ x\ne0\wedge x\ne1$ we have $Z_1=\{0\}$ and
$Z_2=\{1\}$, and neither contains the other; by Theorem C no reduction of the required form exists.

**Corollary 4.3.** *If $n\ge2$ and the sets $Z_1,\dots,Z_n$ are pairwise incomparable under
inclusion (e.g. the solution sets of $x=c_1,\dots,x=c_n$ for pairwise distinct constants
$c_1,\dots,c_n$), then the system $\bigwedge_jL_jx\ne g_j$ admits no reduction to a single inequation
plus an $x$-free condition.*

*Proof.* If some $Z_{j_0}$ contained all $Z_j$, then for any $j\ne j_0$ (such $j$ exists as $n\ge2$)
the sets $Z_j$ and $Z_{j_0}$ would be comparable. So condition (2) of Theorem C fails, hence so does
(1). $\square$

# 5. The repaired formulation, and what to use instead

**(a) Equations.** *Every finite system of linear differential equations in one unknown is
equivalent to a single equation together with an $x$-free compatibility condition:*
$$\bigwedge_{j=1}^{n}L_jx=f_j\iff\Big(Lx=f\ \wedge\ \bigwedge_{j=1}^{n}V_jf=f_j\Big),$$
*where $L=\mathrm{GCRD}(L_1,\dots,L_n)=\sum_jU_jL_j$, $L_j=V_jL$, $f=\sum_jU_jf_j$* (Theorems A, A$'$).
It is better to state the result in this form, exhibiting $U_j,V_j$: the Bézout identity is exactly
what makes *both* implications work, and it also displays $\psi$. If an induction on $n$ is wanted,
use Lemma 2.1 as the merging step.

**(b) Inequations.** *There is no analogue.* By Theorem B a conjunction of inequations is in general
**not** equivalent to a single inequation plus an $x$-free condition, and by Theorem C this happens
only when one inequation already implies the others. In an inductive set-up the inequations must
therefore be kept as a list; all one can do is delete $L_jx\ne g_j$ whenever $Z_j\subseteq Z_{j_0}$
for some other index $j_0$.

**(c) What one can still do with inequations: reduce them modulo the equation.** This is normally the
step such a normal form is wanted for, and it is correct.

**Corollary 5.1.** *Let $L\in K[\partial]$, $L\ne0$, $f\in F$, and let $M_j\in K[\partial]$,
$g_j\in F$ for $1\le j\le m$. Write $M_j=Q_jL+R_j$ with $\deg R_j<\deg L$ (Lemma 1.2). Then for all
$x\in F$*
$$\Big(Lx=f\ \wedge\ \bigwedge_{j=1}^{m}M_jx\ne g_j\Big)\iff
\Big(Lx=f\ \wedge\ \bigwedge_{j=1}^{m}R_jx\ne g_j-Q_jf\Big).$$
*In particular, if $\deg L=0$, say $L=a\in K^{\times}$ (so the equation reads $x=a^{-1}f$), then all
$R_j=0$ and the inequations turn into the $x$-free conditions $0\ne g_j-Q_jf$.*

*Proof.* Fix $x$ with $Lx=f$. For each $j$,
$M_jx=(Q_jL+R_j)x=Q_j(Lx)+R_jx=Q_jf+R_jx$, hence $M_jx\ne g_j\iff R_jx\ne g_j-Q_jf$. Since both
sides of the asserted equivalence contain the conjunct $Lx=f$, and both sides are false when
$Lx\ne f$, the equivalence holds for every $x\in F$. If $\deg L=0$ then $\deg R_j<0$, i.e. $R_j=0$. $\square$

Combining (a) and (c): a mixed system $\bigwedge_iL_ix=f_i\ \wedge\ \bigwedge_jM_jx\ne g_j$ whose
merged operator $L$ of Theorem A$'$ is nonzero (if $L=0$, the equations impose no condition on $x$ at
all and there is nothing to reduce) is equivalent to
$$Lx=f\ \wedge\ \bigwedge_{j}R_jx\ne g_j-Q_jf\ \wedge\ \psi ,$$
with $L,f,\psi$ as in Theorem A$'$ and $\deg R_j<\deg L$: one equation, an $x$-free condition, and
inequations of order strictly smaller than that of the equation. This is the strongest normal form
available, and it is the correct replacement for the second half of the argument in the question.

**(d) Points of formulation.**
* Specify that the operators are **linear**, over which differential field $K$ their coefficients
  are taken, and where $x$ and the data $f_j,g_j$ live (Remark 3.3 and §0). Spell out "$\phi$ can be
  written as $Lx=f\wedge\psi$" as the equivalence (0.1), quantified over all $x$, with the data fixed.
* "We suppose that $\phi:\bigwedge_jL_jx=f_j$ and we assume that $\phi$ can be written as
  $Lx=f\wedge\psi$" reads as though the conclusion were being assumed; it should say "we claim" /
  "we shall show".
* An inductive step must carry the entire previous conclusion, the side condition $\psi$ included;
  the step in the question drops $\psi$ and asserts equivalence with $Lx=f$ alone.
* With base case $n=1$, the phrase "we can reduce the first $k$ equations" is legitimate for $k\ge1$;
  the induction is sound as soon as the merging step is replaced by Lemma 2.1.

# 6. Direct answers to the questions asked

* **"Is the last part correct?"** No. The passage from $\tilde Lx=f_{k+1}+f+a+b$ to
  $\tilde Lx\ne f_{k+1}+f$ is invalid exactly because $a+b$ may vanish; and the statement it is meant
  to prove is itself false (Theorem B).
* **"Do we maybe have to suppose $a,b>0$?"** No; that is not a legitimate move (Remark 3.2): $a,b$
  are functions of $x$, not free parameters; the added hypothesis would strengthen $\phi$ and destroy
  the equivalence; and in a general differential field there is no ordering. Moreover no additional
  hypothesis of this kind could help, since Claim 2 is false, and Theorem C describes precisely the
  (degenerate) cases in which the merging of inequations is possible.
* **"Is everything correct?"** The first claim is true but its proof is not (the summing step —
  Example 2.4 — and the dropping of $\psi$); a correct proof, in the same inductive shape, is
  Theorem A, with the explicit form in Theorem A$'$. The second claim is false: Theorem B, sharpened
  by Theorem C. The usable substitutes are in §5.
